questions.q: Why are WebSockets preferred over HTTP polling for real-time chat delivery?
options: WebSockets compress message payloads far better than HTTP does
A persistent duplex connection lets the server push messages instantly
WebSockets bypass load balancers entirely, reducing network hops
WebSockets guarantee ordered, exactly-once message delivery at the protocol level with built-in acknowledgments
questions.explanation: One long-lived duplex connection lets the server initiate delivery the moment a message arrives, avoiding polling's latency floor and its wasted empty requests.

questions.q: In a chat system, what does a delivered receipt actually indicate?
options: The recipient opened the conversation and viewed the message
The server durably wrote the message to persistent storage
The sender's device confirmed its upload to the gateway finished
The message reached the recipient's device but may be unread
questions.explanation: Delivered means the recipient's client acknowledged receipt of the payload. Whether a human looked at it is a separate, later signal called the read receipt.

questions.q: Which component tracks which gateway server currently holds each user's live connection?
options: A session registry mapping user IDs to their gateway servers
The message queue's consumer-group coordinator service
The CDN's edge routing table for connected regions
A sticky cookie maintained by the load balancer for each user
questions.explanation: A shared registry (often Redis) answers "where is this user connected?", so any node can route a message to the exact gateway holding the recipient's socket.

questions.q: What is the standard way to order messages within a single conversation?
options: Sort by each sender's device clock timestamp at send time
Order by the moment of arrival at the recipient's device
A server-assigned monotonic sequence number per conversation
A global wall-clock timestamp synchronized across devices via NTP
questions.explanation: A single server-side sequence per conversation gives one authoritative total order that every device agrees on, immune to client clock skew and varying network delay.

questions.q: How do messages reach a user whose devices are all offline?
options: They are dropped, and the sender must retry manually later
The gateway holds the socket open until the user returns
Peers resend them directly once both parties come online together
The server stores them in the user's inbox and syncs on reconnect
questions.explanation: Store-and-forward is the core of offline delivery: the server durably persists the message and the client pulls everything past its cursor when it reconnects.

questions.q: With end-to-end encryption enabled, who can read a message's plaintext?
options: The server, briefly, while it routes each message onward
Only sender and recipient devices holding the session keys
Any device that successfully authenticates with the user's password
The push notification provider, so it can render message previews
questions.explanation: In E2EE the keys live only on endpoint devices, so relays and servers move ciphertext they cannot decrypt. That is precisely the property E2EE provides.

questions.q: What purpose do heartbeats serve on chat gateway connections?
options: Detecting dead or half-open connections and keeping presence accurate
Batching many small messages together into fewer network frames to reduce per-message TCP overhead
Re-encrypting the session key on a fixed rotation interval
Synchronizing client clocks so message timestamps stay comparable
questions.explanation: TCP can stay open long after a peer vanishes. Periodic pings expose half-open sockets so the gateway can free resources and mark the user offline promptly.

questions.q: How is a message delivered to all members of a small group chat?
options: The sender's device opens a direct connection to each member
Members poll a shared topic for new messages every few seconds
The server fans out copies to each member's inbox or live connection
The CDN replicates the message into edge caches in each member's home region for faster reads
questions.explanation: Server-side fanout writes to each member's inbox or pushes to their open socket, which handles offline members and keeps clients from needing peer-to-peer connectivity.

questions.q: A user runs the app on a phone and a laptop. How should the system deliver an incoming message?
options: Deliver only to whichever device was most recently active
Fan out to every registered device, each tracking its own sync cursor
Deliver to one device and let it copy the message to the others
Queue the message until all of the user's devices are online simultaneously
questions.explanation: Treating each device as an independent endpoint with its own cursor means every device converges on the full history whenever it comes online, without depending on a peer.

questions.q: The sender is connected to gateway A and the recipient to gateway B. How does the message travel?
options: Gateway A looks up the recipient's gateway and forwards through the routing layer
Gateway A broadcasts the message to every gateway in the cluster, and each one filters for local recipients
The recipient's client periodically polls gateway A for new messages directly
The load balancer migrates the recipient's socket over to gateway A
questions.explanation: A session-registry lookup turns delivery into a targeted hop to the one gateway holding the socket, which scales far better than broadcasting to the whole cluster.

questions.q: In a 200-member group, naive per-message read receipts create a problem. What is it, and the usual mitigation?
options: Receipts leak message plaintext, mitigated by hashing each receipt
Receipts arrive out of order, which is fixed by attaching vector clocks
Receipts double storage costs, which is fixed by TTL-based deletion
Receipt volume scales with readers times messages; use per-user last-read cursors instead
questions.explanation: One receipt per member per message is a multiplicative blowup. Storing a single last-read sequence number per member collapses it to O(members) and still implies everything before.

questions.q: A client's connection drops before it receives a send acknowledgment, so it resends. What prevents a duplicate message?
options: The server compares message text and timestamps to spot repeats
TCP retransmission and sequence numbers already prevent duplicates end to end at the transport layer
A client-generated unique message ID lets the server deduplicate resends
The client waits for the next heartbeat before attempting the resend
questions.explanation: An idempotency key minted by the client survives reconnects, so the server recognizes the retry as the same logical message. TCP guarantees nothing across a new connection.

questions.q: Why does a mobile chat app still need APNs or FCM push even though it uses WebSockets?
options: Push delivers large media attachments faster than sockets can
Push encrypts notification payloads, while sockets cannot
Push costs the server less than maintaining millions of idle sockets
Mobile OSes suspend background connections, so only platform push can wake the app
questions.explanation: iOS and Android reclaim background sockets to save battery, so the OS-level push channel is the only reliable way to reach a backgrounded or killed app.

questions.q: Why is a wide-column store like Cassandra a common choice for chat message history?
options: It handles high write volume with conversation-keyed partitions ordered by message ID
It supports multi-row ACID transactions needed for group conversations
It offers built-in full-text search across all stored message history
It stores media blobs inline more efficiently than object storage does
questions.explanation: Partitioning by conversation with a clustering key on message ID matches the access pattern exactly: append-heavy writes and ordered range reads of recent history.

questions.q: How should typing indicators be handled compared to regular chat messages?
options: Persist them in the inbox alongside messages for auditability
Send them over a dedicated TCP connection with automatic retries and exponential backoff
Treat them as ephemeral fire-and-forget events that may be dropped
Batch them together with read receipts into the message log
questions.explanation: A typing signal is worthless a second later, so durability and retries add cost with no benefit. Dropping them under load degrades gracefully.

questions.q: Why should a conversation not be ordered by sender device timestamps?
options: Timestamps consume too much storage on every message row
Client clocks skew, so a reply can sort before the message it answers
Timestamps collide whenever two users type at the same moment
Encrypted payloads hide the timestamps from the ordering service until each device decrypts them
questions.explanation: Device clocks drift and can be set arbitrarily, so client time gives no causal guarantee and can invert cause and effect in the rendered transcript.

questions.q: A channel grows to 500k members and per-member inbox writes per message become untenable. What is the standard remedy?
options: Read from a single shared conversation log on demand instead of writing per-member copies
Compress each member's inbox copy of the message using delta encoding
Split the channel into fifty independent subchannels behind one name
Move the fanout work onto client devices over mesh networking
questions.explanation: This is fanout-on-read: for huge channels one shared log plus per-member cursors replaces 500k writes per message with a read each member does only when they look.

questions.q: In Signal-style group encryption, why use sender keys instead of pairwise sessions for each message?
options: Sender keys survive device changes without requiring re-registration
Pairwise sessions leak the full group membership list to the server through their session metadata
Sender keys avoid encrypting each message separately for every member
Pairwise sessions are unable to provide any forward secrecy
questions.explanation: Pairwise encryption is O(members) ciphertexts per message. A sender key is distributed once, then each message is encrypted a single time for the whole group.

questions.q: A gateway pushes a message to a socket that silently died before its heartbeat timeout fired. What prevents message loss?
options: TCP guarantees delivery to the client once the write syscall succeeds
The registry always removes dead sockets synchronously with the failure
The operating system buffers the message until the client reconnects
The message is persisted first and only marked delivered on client acknowledgment
questions.explanation: Durable-then-ack means an unacknowledged message stays pending in the inbox and is redelivered on reconnect. A successful socket write proves nothing about client receipt.

questions.q: A user in 300 groups reconnects after a month offline. How do production systems make this sync tractable?
options: Replay the user's entire event stream from account creation onward
Sync recent conversation heads first, then lazily page older history per cursor on open
Reset all conversation cursors and mark the entire backlog as read
Push the full message backlog through APNs in sequence order
questions.explanation: Fetching just the latest message and unread count per conversation makes the list usable in one small round trip, deferring bulk history to the conversations actually opened.
